full_judgment:
2. Short facts relevant for the purpose of the case are that the petitioner as plaintiff instituted Title Suit No. 10 of 1999 in the 2nd Court of Subordinate Judge, Chuadanga against the defendant opposite parties for a declaration that the decision of the Governing Body of Jiban Nagar Degree College placing the petitioner under suspension vide its notification dated 23-8-1999 is illegal, collusive and against the Regulations of the National University and, as such, the same is liable to be struck down. 

 3. The petitioner's case, in short, is that he has been the Principal of Jiban Nagar Degree College for quite a long period and he has been discharging his duty honestly, sincerely, efficiently and to the entire satisfaction of all concerned. It has been alleged that the Chairman of the Governing Body could not see eye to eye with the plaintiff on administrative and academic matters, for which the former bore grudge against the plaintiff and it was the said Chairman, who is no other person than the Deputy Commissioner of Chuadanga, who entered into an unholy conspiracy with others against the plaintiff and passed the impugned order of suspension illegally and arbitrarily and hence the suit. 

 4. The opposite party defendants contested the suit by filing joint written statements denying the material allegations of the plaint and contended, inter alia, that the suit as framed is not maintainable in law. It has been further alleged that the plaintiff by misusing his position as the principal of the College misappropriated funds of the College and committed acts of misconduct by remaining un-authorisedly absent from the College. It has been further stated that the allegations against the plaintiff were enquired into by a Magistrate of the 1st Class and on the basis of the enquiry report filed by the learned Magistrate, the plaintiff was placed under suspension pending the departmental proceeding. 

 5. At the trial, the plaintiff examined one witness while the contesting opposite parties also examined one witness in support of their respective cases. The parties also exhibited a series of documents in support of their claims. 

 6. The learned Subordinate Judge, on consideration of the facts and circumstances of the case and the evidence on record, was pleased by his impugned judgment dated 6-8-2001 to decree the suit on contest. 

 12. The learned Advocate for the petitioner has placed before us the material evidence on record, both oral and documentary, the provision of Article 16 of the terms and conditions of the service of the Teachers of the Degree Colleges under the National University as well as the impugned judgments passed by the learned Courts below. It is found that the learned Subordinate Judged duly considered all material aspects of the case and the material evidence on record, both oral and documentary, and decreed the suit on the finding that the impugned order of suspension is illegal and malafide. The learned Court of appeal below dismissed the suit and reversed the judgment of the trial Court on the only ground that suspension being a temporary measure pending a departmental proceeding, the suit challenging an order of suspension is not maintainable in law. 

 14. The Service Regulations thus provide that the Governing Body of a Degree College under the National University can take appropriate punitive action against a delinquent teacher defined on grounds of professional misconduct or moral turpitude under certain circumstances. Article 16(ka) of the Regulations provides that the allegations of misconduct or moral turpitude shall have to be enquired into by a specially constituted committee consisting of five members, including a teacher of the College and representative of the University. Article (Ga) of the relevant Regulations provides that if the delinquent teacher is to be "placed under suspension pending the departmental enquiry, he shall have to be given 50/ of the monthly salary as subsistence allowance during the period of the enquiry. In the instant case, it is found that the impugned order was passed by the Governing Body of the College on 23-8-99 without forming an enquiry committee as enjoined by Article 16(Ka) of the University Regulations. It is found from the record that an enquiry committee was subsequently formed on 22-9-99 ie one month after placing the plaintiff under suspension on 23-8-99. 

 15. The impugned order of suspension dated 22-8-99 has been marked as Exhibit I while the relevant University Regulations regulating the terms and conditions of service of the College Teachers under the National University has been marked as Exhibit 3. The Resolution book of Jibgan Nagar Degree College has been marked as Exhibit 4. There is absolutely nothing on record to show that the college authority did take action against the plaintiff-petitioner in pursuance of the enquiry report dated 8-8-2000 allegedly submitted by the Enquiry Committee. In such circumstances, we are not in a position to hold as to whether the enquiry was conducted in conformity with the requirements of law on giving necessary opportunity to the plaintiff to defend him. It is thus evident that the impugned order of suspension dated 23-8-99 has not been followed by taking any meaningful endeavour towards successful culmination of the departmental enquiry within a reasonable time. It is unfortunate that the impugned order of suspension dated 23-8-99 has been in force for over 3 years without being attended with further actions for completing the department proceeding against the plaintiff. The inexcusable failure of the College Governing Body in conducting a meaningful and effective enquiry and to take appropriate action thereon evidently proves the utter callousness and inept inability of the defendant opposite parties in dealing with the fate of the plaintiff-petitioner, who has been kept under suspension for over three years without paying him even a single farthing and subsistence allowance as envisaged by Articles 16(ga) of the University Regulations Exhibit 1 This seemingly animated hibernation of an over Zealous College Governing Body of over three years is the clearest manifestation of acts of high-handedness, recklessness and irresponsibility. In the facts and circumstances of the case and the evidence on record, we have no hesitation in accepting the argument of Mr Nandy that the impugned order of suspension is malafide and is the product of colorable exercise of power for collateral purposes. 

 16. In the circumstances of the case the Court is certainly entitled to look into the legality and propriety of the impugned order of suspension, which is not only illegal and malafide but is also oppressive in nature and content. 

 17. Mr Harendra Nath Nandy has referred to us the case of Abdul Hashim vs Chairman National Board of Revenue, Dhaka and another reported in 32 DLR 55, the case of Altaf Hossain vs Md Abdul Rahim and others, reported in 51 DLR 527 and the case of AK Joinul Abedin vs Sayeeder Rahman and others reported in 1982 BLD 51 in support of his contentions. 

 18. The ratio decidendi of these decisions is that although suspension is not a punishment and it can be resorted to in connection with a departmental proceeding already drawn up or about to be drawn up, yet it cannot be resorted by way of punishment when the Court finds the move malafide and arbitrary, it is not only competent to look into the legality and propriety of the impugned action but is also called upon to act decisively to administer even-handed justice. The failure of the defendant opposite parties to make out any case for professional misconduct or moral turpitude following departmental proceeding against the plaintiff-petitioner in the course of the last 3 years and the attending circumstances of the case unerringly prove that the impugner, order of suspension is malafide and for collateral purposes. It hardly needs any emphasis to state that law does not protect any malafide or arbitrary act because such act by its very nature is illegal and without jurisdiction. It cannot, therefore, be laid down as an inflexible proposition that 'suspension', though purely a temporary measure by the employer or the controlling authority pending a departmental enquiry against a delinquent employee, is immune from judicial scrutiny. In an appropriate case, the Court can certainly adjudicate upon its legality and justifiability to prevent an injustice. 

 19. We have already noticed that the order of suspension was passed against the petitioner more than three years ago but till today the College' authority has failed to bring the inauspicious" proceeding to a meaningful conclusion. This attitude of the College Governing Body is shockingly deplorable and highly deprecated. The allegation of professional misconduct or moral turpitude against the plaintiff-petitioner has not been proved at all and falls to the ground automatically. 

 20. In the facts of the case and the materials on record, we are of the firm view that the suit as framed is maintainable in law and the plaintiff is entitled to the reliefs prayed for. The learned Subordinate Judge duly considered the material evidence on record and found the impugned order of suspension as illegal and malafide. The impugned judgment passed by the learned Subordinate Judge is found to be well supported by the evidence on record. The learned District Judge on a mechanical view of law and on erroneous assumption of facts dismissed the suit without at all considering the attending facts and circumstances of the case and the material evidence on record and the same has indeed occasioned failure of justice. We, therefore, find sufficient ground "to interfere with the impugned judgment and decree passel by the learned District Judge, Chuadanga in Title Appeal No. 73 of 2001. 

 22. The plaintiff-petitioner filed an application before this Court praying for a mandatory injunction directing Jibon Nagar College Governing Body to pay the arrear dues to the plaintiff, including all Government benefits, during the period of his suspension. In the facts of the case, we do not find such an order necessary, as the petitioner is entitled under the law to get all his legitimate dues all through as the Principal of the College.
